nodes.label: Doctrine of stare decisis: like cases must be decided alike, courts bound by decisions of higher courts
Ratio decidendi: the legal reasoning/principle that forms the binding part of a judgment
Obiter dicta: comments made 'by the way' in a judgment, not binding but persuasive
Hierarchy of the courts (England and Wales): Supreme Court, Court of Appeal (Civil/Criminal Division), High Court, Crown Court, Magistrates'/County Court
Supreme Court: position at the top of the hierarchy and use of the Practice Statement 1966 to depart from its own past decisions
Court of Appeal bound by Supreme Court and generally bound by its own past decisions (Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co exceptions)
Binding precedent: a decision from a higher (or same, per rules) court that a later court must follow
Persuasive precedent: not binding but may be followed, e.g. obiter dicta, lower court decisions, dissenting judgments, decisions of other jurisdictions/Privy Council
Original precedent: a decision on a point of law that has never been decided before, forming new law
Overruling: a higher court (or same court using Practice Statement) states that a legal rule decided in an earlier case is wrong
Reversing: a higher court on appeal in the same case overturns the decision of the lower court below it
Distinguishing: a court finds material differences between the facts of the current case and a previous precedent, avoiding being bound
Advantage of precedent: certainty - lawyers/clients can predict outcomes and advise accordingly
Advantage of precedent: consistency and fairness - like cases treated alike, promoting justice
Advantage of precedent: flexibility - mechanisms such as distinguishing, overruling and the Practice Statement allow the law to develop
Advantage of precedent: precision - detailed application of law to specific facts builds a large body of precise rules
Advantage of precedent: time-saving - lawyers and judges do not need to reargue settled points of law in every case
Disadvantage of precedent: rigidity - lower courts must follow binding precedent even if it seems wrong, unless it can be distinguished
Disadvantage of precedent: complexity and volume of case law makes it hard to find the correct ratio, especially in cases with multiple judgments
Disadvantage of precedent: slowness of change - the law can only develop when a suitable case reaches the appellate courts
Disadvantage of precedent: distinguishing can be used artificially/illogically, creating fine and unprincipled distinctions between cases
Disadvantage of precedent: retrospective effect - overruling changes the law after the events in question occurred, undermining certainty for past conduct
Reasons law reform is needed: society, technology and values change, and gaps/inconsistencies/outdated rules must be addressed
Law Commission: permanent independent body established by the Law Commissions Act 1965 to review and recommend reform of the law
Law Commission's functions: codification, consolidation, repeal of obsolete law, and reducing the number of separate statutes
Law Commission's process: research and consultation (consultation papers), production of reports with draft Bills for Parliament
Other law reform mechanisms: Royal Commissions, ad hoc advisory committees and Parliamentary committees inquiring into specific issues
Advantage of law reform bodies: independence and expertise - research conducted by legal specialists free from political pressure
Advantage of law reform bodies: thorough research and public consultation produce well-considered, evidence-based reforms
Advantage of law reform bodies: codification and consolidation work simplifies and modernises the law, improving accessibility
Advantage of law reform bodies: comprehensive review of whole areas of law rather than piecemeal change
Disadvantage of law reform bodies: lack of enforcement power - Parliament is not obliged to implement Law Commission recommendations
Disadvantage of law reform bodies: delay - the process of research, consultation and drafting is slow, and implementation may take years or never happen
Disadvantage of law reform bodies: lack of Parliamentary time to debate and pass recommended reform Bills amid competing legislative priorities
Disadvantage of law reform bodies: cost of running research, consultation and reporting processes funded by the taxpayer
UK membership of the EU (1973-2020) and the framework of EU law applying within England and Wales during that period
European Commission: proposes new legislation, oversees implementation of EU law and represents the EU's interests
Council of the European Union (Council of Ministers): represents member states' governments and, with Parliament, adopts legislation
European Parliament: directly elected body that debates and, with the Council, adopts legislation and scrutinises the Commission
Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU): interprets EU law, ensures its uniform application and rules on disputes between institutions/member states
Treaties as a source of EU law: primary source setting out fundamental principles, directly applicable in member states
Regulations as a source of EU law: directly applicable in all member states without the need for national implementing legislation
Directives as a source of EU law: set a result to be achieved, requiring member states to pass their own implementing legislation within a set time limit
Decisions as a source of EU law: binding only on the specific member state(s), companies or individuals to which they are addressed
Supremacy of EU law: Costa v ENEL established that EU law took precedence over conflicting national law of member states
Direct effect: EU law provisions (e.g. Treaty Articles, Regulations) create rights individuals can rely on directly in national courts (Van Gend en Loos)
Vertical direct effect: individuals can enforce EU law rights against the state/emanations of the state
Horizontal direct effect: individuals can enforce certain EU law rights against other private individuals/bodies
European Communities Act 1972: gave EU law direct effect and incorporated it into UK domestic law, including s.2(4) requiring UK courts to interpret statutes consistently with EU law
Impact of EU law on UK statutory interpretation: UK courts required to interpret domestic legislation purposively to comply with EU law obligations
Impact of EU law on Parliamentary sovereignty: EU law's supremacy limited Parliament's ability to legislate contrary to EU obligations while a member
Impact of EU law on judicial precedent: UK courts bound to follow CJEU rulings on interpretation of EU law, affecting domestic precedent during membership
Impact of Brexit/European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018: retained EU law converted into domestic law, ending automatic supremacy and direct effect of new EU law
